podcasts.name: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Enduring Presence
podcast.body: Hailing from Sweden, The Hives are noted as one of the bands from the early 2000s indie rock revival that are "still with us," indicating their continued activity and relevance in the music scene. "The hives are still with us."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 9: (20-11)

podcast.title: Indie Rock Revival (2000s)
podcast.body: The Hives are listed among the "fresh sounding bands" that appeared as part of the Indie Rock Revival in the early 2000s, revitalizing interest in various genres.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Dreampop - A History

podcast.title: Influence on Andre 3000
podcast.body: This "new early 2000s garage rock band from Sweden" was cited by Andre 3000 as an influence for Outcast's biggest hit, "Hey Y'all," contributing to its genre-blending power pop sound. "And a new early 2000s garage rock band from Sweden called The Hives."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Shake It Like a Polaroid Picture Edition Part 2

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Shake It Like a Polaroid Picture Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Influenced by The Stooges
podcast.body: The Hives would likely list The Stooges as a group that influenced their sound. "If you were to ask a contemporary band like, say, the white stripes or the hives about which groups influence their sound, they would probably list off a bunch of names including the stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Stooges?

podcast.title: Major Label Deal with Alan McGee
podcast.body: In 2000, following their second album, "Vini Vidi Vicious," The Hives were signed by Alan McGee, the founder of Creation Records (who discovered Oasis), to his new label, Pop Tones. This deal led to a major label contract that some speculated was worth $50 million. "By 2000, Alan McGee had a new label called Pop Tones and he wanted The Hives. So he signed them. One thing led to another and suddenly, the Hives had a major label deal that some said was worth $50 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Origin and Longevity
podcast.body: The Hives originated from Fagersta, Sweden, and had been active in various forms since 1989, prior to gaining wider recognition in the early 2000s. "They were from Feggers to Sweden and had been hanging around in some form or another since 1989."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 2: The Indie Revolution

podcast.title: Part of Indy Rock Revival
podcast.body: The Hives were explicitly named as a band that, alongside The Strokes, The White Stripes, the Yeah Yeah Yeahs, Interpol, The Vines, and Arcade Fire, was a firm part of the Indy Rock Revival in the late 2003/early 2004 period. "The strokes were firmly part of the Indy Rock Revival that also included the white stripes, the yay-yayas, interpole, the vines, the hives, and this new band called Arcade Fire."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Strokes

podcast.title: Pioneers of the Indie Rock Revival (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: The Hives were among the "new, sharp clever bands" that emerged during the Indie Rock Revival or Post-Punk Revival period around 2000-2001. This movement was a refurbished version of old-school early alt-rock, garage rock, and punk styles. "We gave us new, sharp clever bands like the strokes and the hives, the yay-yaz, friends ferdinand, interpool, and the arctic monkeys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Raw Indie Rock Scene Association
podcast.body: The Hives are considered part of the "raw indie rock scene," often grouped with bands like The Vines, The Strokes, The Datsuns, and The Doves. "part of that whole raw indie rock scene."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rocks Craziest People

podcast.title: Sweden's Sharpest Dressed Band
podcast.body: The Hives are acclaimed as potentially Sweden's sharpest dressed band, known for their unwavering commitment to a black and white color palette. Their outfits consistently feature variations such as black shirts with white satin ties, black pants, and white shoes, or the inverse, making their monochrome aesthetic a distinctive signature. "And there are the hives, who just might be Sweden's sharpest dress band. The clothes may change, but the palette remains the same. Black and white. Black shirts, white satin ties, black pants, white shoes, or maybe vice versa, whatever, is always a variation on black and white."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Fashion

podcast.title: Swedish Origins and Sound Pivot
podcast.body: Formed in Sweden in 1989, The Hives significantly pivoted their sound in 1993 to a very "garage-y" style. This stylistic shift preceded their breakthrough success in the early 2000s. "They are Swedish and were formed in 1989. But in 1993, there was a big pivot in their sound to something very garage-y."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Discovered by Alan McGee
xref.body: Oasis is mentioned as the band famously discovered by Alan McGee, who was the founder of Creation Records. McGee later founded Pop Tones and signed The Hives. "Now, you might remember him as the founder of Creation Records and the guy who discovered a Vicious."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: Early Influences & Recognition
xref.body: The Stooges are frequently cited as a major influence by contemporary bands like The White Stripes and The Hives, and by 90s bands such as Jane's Addiction and Nirvana. They also shaped the sound of 80s bands like Sonic Youth and inspired 70s artists like the Sex Pistols, Ramones, and David Bowie to make music. "So the stooges seem to be on everybody's list even though they hardly sold any records in their day and were so messed up that their singer ended up in an asylum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
